docs.title: Framework overview
docs.text:
CellsWeb RPC organizes applications around typed functions and explicit middleware rather than a separate HTTP route for each operation. HTTP carries one envelope; input/output schemas describe contracts and the server keeps authentication state in middleware-owned context.

Capability Node implementation Functions Co-located constants/run/middlewares/tests; nested namespace discovery Validation TypeBox input/output contracts, nullable unions and physical file helpers Middleware Sequential attachments, header/options validation, server-owned context HTTP Native Node, Bun, Express, Fastify, Hono, Elysia, Ultimate Express Uploads JSON/multipart, routing consistency, per-request limits and temporary-file cleanup Frontend Standalone client, React provider/query/mutation hooks, React Native URI assets Developer tooling Generators, in-process tests, worker opt-in and interactive docs

The packages have distinct responsibilities:

  • rpc-core: server and local CLI.
  • rpc-client: browser/mobile/Node client.
  • create-cellsweb-rpc-api: project initializer.
  • Go runtime: native engine with shared logical contracts.

Choose function-oriented RPC for shared application contracts and upload-heavy clients. CellsWeb RPC is not GraphQL query selection, gRPC streaming or an identity provider. Runtime/schema differences between Node and Go remain explicit; semantic parity does not mean identical implementation or every error detail.

Build schema-validated RPC functions with a shared middleware pipeline across Node/Bun HTTP adapters. See release status and installation for core 1.0.35, client 1.0.26 and scaffolder 1.0.31.

  • Functions and schemas
  • Middleware and authentication
  • Client/React and multipart uploads
  • Seven adapters and global docs controls
  • CLI, testing, workers
  • Protocol, API reference, Go sibling

Node 24 LTS is primary; declared Node floor 24.0.0 is tested directly. Bun is tested independently. The deprecated isPublic property is ignored, and auth is enforced by middleware rather than documentation metadata.

docs.title: For contributors
docs.text: Start with contribution policy, development setup and the internal source map. The sidebar separates end-user usage from implementation, testing and release guides. See the security policy and Code of Conduct before opening a report.

docs.title: Start an application
docs.text:
npm create cellsweb-rpc-api@latest my-api -- --framework=node --yes --pm=npm
cd my-api
npm run typecheck
npm run build
npm test
npm run dev

The generated public.hello route accepts {name:"Ada"}. Add functions and middleware with the project-local CLI, then use the HTTP SDK or React provider in your frontend. Read functions, client, uploads and adapters for full examples.

Native stream intake and Fetch formData have different buffering boundaries. Schemas, authentication, output checks and cleanup remain part of the pipeline. See execution lifecycle and source architecture when contributing.

docs.title: Server adapters
docs.text:
The seven complete generated templates are the tested integration examples. Generate each with --framework=<name> rather than copying an incomplete body parser or converting binary buffers through strings.

Template Runtime Integration node Node 24 http.createServer with awaited CoreRPC.createHandler express Node 24 native request/response handler fastify Node 24 fastifyPlugin; scoped multipart stream parser ultimate-express Node 24 native handler; framework-specific end/close lifecycle hono Node 24 with @hono/node-server CoreRPC.fetch via createHonoHandler bun Bun Fetch handler/Bun.serve elysia Bun Fetch handler with adapter parse behavior 
import http from 'node:http';
import { CoreRPC } from '@cellsweb/rpc-core';
export async function nodeServer() {
  const rpc = new CoreRPC({ functionsDir: './dist/functions', middlewaresDir: './dist/middlewares', docs: false });
  return { rpc, server: http.createServer(await rpc.createHandler()) };
}

There is no init() method. For Fastify register rpc.fastifyPlugin(); it keeps multipart stream parsing within the plugin scope, preserving JSON parsing. For Hono apply the factory to the Hono instance: rpc.honoPlugin()(honoApp). For Elysia .use(rpc.elysiaPlugin()) is the plugin factory; the generated full template additionally handles static binary responses. Follow the tested templates when mounting complete services.

rpc.fetch(request) accepts a Web Request. Documentation uses its parsed pathname so queries/absolute URLs do not break details. Native and Fetch intake share logical contracts but buffering/lifecycle differ. Hono's tested host here is Node, not Cloudflare/Deno/Edge: CoreRPC discovery uses Node filesystem APIs. No unsupported Edge deployment guarantee is implied by a Fetch-shaped handler.

Keep multipart routing headers/body redundant and consistent. Do not consume a multipart stream in unrelated middleware before CRPC. See uploads and global docs controls; production guards apply to all seven generated templates. Application errors retain default HTTP 200 envelopes.

docs.title: Public API reference
docs.text:
This describes core 1.0.35 and client 1.0.26 exports (unchanged runtime APIs). See installation and the generated package declarations.

@cellsweb/rpc-core exports CoreRPC, CoreRpcOptions, middleware/registry types, AppError/ErrorCode, createTestCaller, UploadedFile, File/Files, FormNum/FormBool, schema validation and adapter helpers. The generated .d.ts files are the exact API reference; examples in functions and middleware are compiled against those declarations.

docs.title: CoreRPC
docs.text:
Options include functionsDir, middlewaresDir, rpcEndpoint, docsEndpoint, healthEndpoint, host, port, docs, strict, cors, trustProxy, useHttpStatusCodes, onTelemetry. Explicit options win over their implemented environment defaults.

Method Purpose getRegistry() Load/access discovered functions and middleware createHandler() Await a Node request/response handler fetch(Request) Dispatch Web requests start(port?) Start native Node HTTP close() Close framework-owned server/workers execute(key,data,options?) In-memory envelope execution fastifyPlugin(), honoPlugin(), elysiaPlugin() Adapter factories serveBun(port?) Start under Bun

There is no exported Context alias or init() lifecycle. Use MiddlewareContext. MiddlewareFn receives its params object and context; it returns a context. See adapters for actual factory mounting and buffering qualifications.

docs.title: Errors, files and clients
docs.text:
Handled application errors use {status:'error',code,message,details?} with HTTP 200 by default; success is {status:'ok',data,meta?}. Opt-in HTTP mapping, transport failures, custom routes and docs404 are separate. AppError is the server error; RpcError is the client error. Telemetry reports requestId, durationMs, status and optional namespace/function/code/message/clientIp/userAgent/error fields.

UploadedFile properties: path, filename, byteLength, mimeType, declaredMimeType, detectedMimeType. Methods: createReadStream, toBuffer, toBlob. Avoid obsolete filepath/mimetype/size examples; Go's file API instead uses native methods.

@cellsweb/rpc-client exports createRpcClient, RpcClient, rawRpcRequest, RpcError and request/response types. React is at /react, with RpcProvider, useRpcClient, useRpcQuery and useRpcMutation. Hooks take options objects, not positional route arguments. See the client guide for compiling examples.

FunctionMetadata.isPublic?:boolean is retained, deprecated and ignored. It controls no docs visibility, authentication or execution. No replacement flag exists; global docs configuration and application middleware are independent.

docs.title: Architecture and protocol
docs.text:
HTTP RPC dispatch uses one configured endpoint, normally POST /rpc:

{"namespace":"public","functionName":"hello","data":{"name":"Alice"}}

Success is {status:'ok',data,meta?}; application errors are {status:'error',code,message,details?}. Default handled application errors use HTTP 200. useHttpStatusCodes:true opts into status mapping. Transport/framing failures, custom HTTP routes and disabled/unknown documentation paths have their own statuses. HTTP 200 is not a proxy-cache/security guarantee; configure caches and monitoring for the actual envelope and route policy.

JSON objects, arrays, scalars and explicit null preserve their shape. Omitted HTTP data defaults to {}; schema validation decides whether it is accepted. Middleware authenticates/authorizes before handler execution. Input and output validation remain active; no remote session/context bypass is provided.

Native Node intake streams JSON/multipart with bounded handling of rejected bodies. Fetch formData can buffer at its runtime boundary. Go fasthttp is transport-buffered before application multipart processing. Per-request limits and cleanup do not establish a zero-allocation or aggregate-memory guarantee.

Multipart requires both accelerated routing headers or neither, exact header/body agreement and routing text before files for headerless fallback. Only top-level files/direct arrays are supported. MIME detection is heuristic, not sanitization.

Node TypeBox and Go native schemas have semantic overlap, not identical keyword, number or error-detail behavior. Node JSON.parse and Go HTTP JSON v2 differ on duplicate members; large integer and omitted-output conventions need explicit application contracts. See the sibling Go guide for bounded IPC 2 MiB framing and no-replay failure handling.

Documentation is globally configured and never grants access to functions. Deprecated isPublic is ignored; middleware owns auth. Public schema projections omit configured middleware values/defaults but cannot classify secrets placed intentionally in public descriptions or constraints.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Benchmark workloads and historical results are maintained in the repository's benchmarks/README.md and benchmarks/RESULTS.md. Record commit, runtime, hardware, concurrency, payload, limits and warmup when comparing results.

Those numbers are workload observations, not current guarantees of latency, throughput, memory, security or adapter superiority. This release's gates are correctness, real HTTP uploads/cleanup, clean installations and schema/auth behavior. No new performance benchmark was executed for the release stabilization work. Go transport buffering and Fetch formData buffering must be accounted for in memory comparisons; see architecture.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
The scaffolder creates a project; @cellsweb/rpc-core supplies its runtime crpc binary. Both packages expose that bin name, so use the project-local core CLI for development/builds rather than relying on global install ordering.

Use the public initializer:

npx create-cellsweb-rpc-api@1.0.31 my-api --framework=fastify --yes
cd my-api
npm run create:function -- --ns catalog --name get --contentType json
npm run create:middleware -- --name tenantResolver --description 'Resolve tenant'
npm run typecheck
npm run build
npm start

The equivalent npm initializer is npm create cellsweb-rpc-api@latest. --skip-install leaves dependency installation to you. See the contributor release guide for intentionally testing unpublished local changes.

crpc dev [entry] runs a TS watcher; crpc build runs tsc then tsc-alias with emitted-extension resolution; crpc start [entry] executes production JS. The generated project's devDependencies supply those tools. Bun execution is selected when the CLI itself runs under Bun; preserve the selected template/runtime.

Function generation also supports JSON batch specs (--batch/--file). Node's function CLI accepts --middlewares; Go's CLI does not share every flag—attach Go middleware in the generated declaration file. Check each tool's own usage. crpc test, test:watch, test:coverage, test:audit invoke configured Vitest commands; the audit command is a test-report convenience, not security certification.

docs.title: Client SDK and React
docs.text:
Install @cellsweb/rpc-client@1.0.26 from npm. React is optional and has its own @cellsweb/rpc-client/react entry. The package supplies JSON and multipart callers; see installation.

import { createRpcClient, RpcError } from '@cellsweb/rpc-client';
export const rpc = createRpcClient({ baseUrl: 'http://localhost:4000/rpc',
  defaultHeaders: () => ({ authorization: 'Bearer replace-with-current-credential' }) });
export async function hello(name: string) {
  try { return await rpc.request<{ greeting: string }>({ namespace: 'public', functionName: 'hello', data: { name } }); }
  catch (error) { if (error instanceof RpcError) console.error(error.code, error.details); throw error; }
}

request unwraps successful data and throws RpcError for structured RPC failures. Forward current credentials via headers, not a caller-supplied trusted context. Do not infer application success solely from HTTP 200. rawRpcRequest is also a standalone unwrapped caller; its name does not mean it returns the raw envelope.

docs.title: Multipart fetch configuration
docs.text:
Client1.0.25 makes standard browser FormData use the configured fetchFn even when XMLHttpRequest exists. Client1.0.24 selected XHR whenever available and bypassed browser multipart fetch wrappers; upgrade the client to obtain the fix.

A web fetch wrapper can supply credentials and intercept multipart requests:

const rpcWithCookies = createRpcClient({
  baseUrl: 'https://api.example.com/rpc',
  fetchFn: (url, init) => fetch(url, { ...init, credentials: 'include' }),
});

Cross-origin cookies also require the server's appropriate CORS configuration. Preserve the supplied headers, body and signal in wrappers; use new Headers when editing headers. Never supply a manual multipart Content-Type/boundary. Timeout, abort and structured RPC error handling remain the client's responsibility.

React Native bridge FormData with getParts() retains the existing XHR path for native URI-file compatibility, so fetchFn does not intercept that path. Configure credentials through defaultHeaders/per-request headers there. No runtime global marker, new transport option or upload-progress API is introduced. Top-level files/direct arrays remain supported and nested files remain rejected.

import type { ReactNode } from 'react';
import { createRpcClient } from '@cellsweb/rpc-client';
import { RpcProvider, useRpcQuery, useRpcMutation } from '@cellsweb/rpc-client/react';
const rpc = createRpcClient({ baseUrl: 'http://localhost:4000/rpc' });
export function Provider({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) { return <RpcProvider client={rpc}>{children}</RpcProvider>; }
export function Greeting({ name }: { name: string }) {
  const query = useRpcQuery<{ greeting: string }, { name: string }>({ namespace: 'public', functionName: 'hello', data: { name } });
  const mutation = useRpcMutation<{ greeting: string }, { name: string }>({ namespace: 'public', functionName: 'hello' });
  return <button disabled={query.loading || mutation.loading} onClick={() => { void mutation.mutate({ name }).catch(console.error); }}>{query.data?.greeting ?? 'Load greeting'}</button>;
}

Hooks accept one options object. Query returns data, loading, error, refetch; mutation returns mutate, loading, error, reset. Await mutate() for its response data; store that result in application state if needed. Hooks require RpcProvider. Query deduplication/re-render ordering does not replace server-side authorization or idempotency handling. Use multipart explicitly for file requests; never manually omit/mismatch the generated routing fields.

docs.title: Our Pledge
docs.text:
We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, caste, color, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

docs.title: Our Standards
docs.text:
Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our community include:

  • Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
  • Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
  • Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
  • Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience
  • Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

  • The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind
  • Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
  • Public or private harassment
  • Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission
  • Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

docs.title: Enforcement Responsibilities
docs.text:
Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation decisions when appropriate.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text:
Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported to the community leaders responsible for enforcement at info@cellsweb.com or the CellsWeb contact page. All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.

docs.title: Enforcement Guidelines
docs.text: Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

docs.title: 1. Correction
docs.text:
Community Impact: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

Consequence: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

docs.title: 2. Warning
docs.text:
Community Impact: A violation through a single incident or series of actions.

Consequence: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

docs.title: 3. Temporary Ban
docs.text:
Community Impact: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior.

Consequence: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period. Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

docs.title: 4. Permanent Ban
docs.text:
Community Impact: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

Consequence: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the community.

docs.title: Contributing to CellsWeb RPC Node
docs.text: Welcome. Small corrections, reproducible bug reports, tests and focused features are useful contributions. Read the Code of Conduct and security policy. Security-sensitive reports must be private. See the MIT LICENSE before including third-party material.

docs.title: Node development setup
docs.text:
Validated toolchain: Node 24.15.0 (declared/tested floor24.0.0), pnpm 11.0.8, TypeScript 7.0.2 from the lockfile and Bun 1.3.11 for Bun/Elysia. Go 1.27.4 is needed when reproducing Go interoperability. Full adapter checks were validated on macOSarm64; report your OS and any platform limitations explicitly.

git clone https://github.com/CellsWeb/crpc-node.git
cd crpc-node
npm install --global pnpm@11.0.8
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm build
pnpm typecheck
pnpm test
pnpm --filter @cellsweb/rpc-core test:types

Use a fork for submission and a focused branch such as docs/request-lifecycle or fix/multipart-boundary. Existing local edits should stay intact; a separate Git worktree is useful when reproducing a pinned baseline. The repo does not pin a packageManager field; use the documented tested pnpm rather than assuming any older pnpm can read current workspace settings.

docs.title: Node repository map and conventions
docs.text:
• packages/rpc-core: CoreRPC, registry, pipeline, request parsers, files, workers, renderer and the runtime crpc CLI. Public exports are in src/index.ts.
  • packages/rpc-client: request/envelope handling, multipart serialization and optional React entrypoint. Keep browser/RN behavior distinct from Node engines.
  • packages/create-cellsweb-rpc-api: initializer, template tree and seven servers.
  • example: reference application and application-level tests; benchmarks: workloads, not a production performance guarantee. docs/ and root mkdocs.yml define the docs site.

Follow the surrounding TypeScript style and strict compiler settings. Preserve TSchema/Static relationships and public ESM/CommonJS declaration identities. Avoid any/ts-ignore merely to make tests compile. Keep handlers transport-neutral; only multipart intake may apply transport-specific schema-directed coercion.

docs.title: Create a Node function or middleware
docs.text:
In the reference/generated application, the project-local core CLI is available:

cd example
pnpm create:function -- --ns catalog --name get --contentType json
pnpm create:middleware -- --name tenantResolver --description 'Resolve tenant'

Review generated constants.ts, run.ts, middlewares.ts and tests. Functions live under src/functions/<namespace>/<function>; middleware under src/middlewares/<name>. Use defineMiddlewares attachments explicitly and implement real verification. Changes to generators require generated-project tests, not just template searches. Scaffold into a disposable app when experimenting instead of committing demo routes.

docs.title: Test and regression workflow
docs.text:
For a bug, pin a baseline, add a behavioral test and record its failing command before fixing implementation. Assert returned data/envelopes and forbidden handler execution, not just HTTP200. Include interruption/cleanup and limit cases for I/O. Focused examples from the repository root:

pnpm --filter @cellsweb/rpc-core exec vitest run src/union-validation.test.ts
pnpm --filter @cellsweb/rpc-core exec vitest run src/docs-parity.test.ts
pnpm --filter @cellsweb/rpc-client test
pnpm --filter create-cellsweb-rpc-api test

Run build/typecheck/full tests for runtime or generator changes. test:types is an explicit clean npm-pack/install integration check and requires registry access. The scaffolder suite executes real seven-adapter builds and HTTP/multipart probes; Bun and the supported native adapter dependencies must be available. Report skips or unavailable tooling; do not turn an omitted suite into a claimed pass.

docs.title: Changes involving both runtimes
docs.text:
Use semantic parity, not identical implementation. Read the sibling Go contributor guide. Propose protocol/default/public-API changes before implementation; identify the migration/version implications. Attach equivalent logical fixtures and actual results for Node and Go. Go's checked-in pkg/rpc/testdata/http-json-shapes.json is a useful fixture set, with HTTP tests in that package and Node union regressions in rpc-core. There is no checked-in one-command cross-repository parity runner; do not require a private review-kit path from external contributors.

Preserve these compatibility boundaries unless explicitly reviewed/versioned:

  • One configurable RPC endpoint with {namespace,functionName,data}. Arbitrary JSON data shapes survive; omitted HTTP data defaults to {}, explicit null stays null for schema validation. Do not silently coerce ordinary JSON inputs.
  • Successfully handled application errors use HTTP200 by default. Opt-in status mapping and transport/framework errors are distinct; not every malformed body automatically produces HTTP400. Preserve success/error envelopes and SDK parsing.
  • Middleware owns authentication/authorization. Remote callers cannot skip it or inject trusted state. Missing configured middleware fails closed.
  • Multipart routing headers come as a pair and agree with required body routing. Headerless fallback puts routing fields before files. No application-owned upload files before required authorization, and no cleanup/size-limit weakening.
  • Client files are top-level fields/direct arrays; nested file objects require a deliberate versioned design. Native Node streams, Fetch form parsing and Go transport buffering have different memory boundaries; do not promise zero RAM.
  • Node discovery and Go registration are intentionally different. isPublic/IsPublic remain deprecated/ignored compatibility fields; no replacement visibility flag.
  • IPC request IDs/framing remain compatible; never replay a failed call implicitly. Unix framing limits do not apply automatically to stdio.

docs.title: Pull requests and review
docs.text:
Open an issue/discussion first for a substantial architectural/API change. Keep one root cause per fix and include problem, before/after behavior, affected paths, compatibility and limitations. Conventional-style subjects such as fix:, docs: and test: help scanning; match existing style without rewriting unrelated files.

Use the PR template. Provide exact executed commands/outcomes, red/green evidence for bugs and both-runtime results where applicable. Docs-only PRs should run both strict MkDocs builds when shared content changes, validate links, render diagrams and compile meaningful examples; unnecessary implementation-mirroring tests are not required. Include screenshots for documentation UI changes. State untested scenarios/skips honestly. Never commit secrets, generated upload files, dist, node_modules, local workspaces or unrelated agent changes.

A maintainer reviews scope, protocol/API impact, tests, resource cleanup and docs before merge. Do not merge/publish/tag as part of an ordinary contribution. Release changes require separate approval and public-install verification. New public API fields/options and defaults require explicit compatibility review.

The contributor documentation contains source maps, request lifecycle, subsystem test maps and release guidance.

docs.title: Go interoperability
docs.text:
Node and Go share the HTTP request shape and default application-error envelopes. Go v1.0.2 includes bounded stdio framing and the earlier hardening fixes. Install github.com/CellsWeb/crpc-go/cmd/crpc-go@v1.0.2 for a CLI that generates the matching SDK dependency. Local workspaces are for deliberate SDK development.

Both runtimes preserve explicit HTTP null and default omitted HTTP data to {}. TypeBox unions and native Go optional/nullable schemas still have different vocabularies. Shared fixtures cover logical shapes/auth/validation, not every JSON Schema keyword, numeric boundary or serialization detail.

The Go repository's verified example-node/src/client.ts is the Unix IPC client. Forward credentials in headers. Anonymous connection errors and malformed JSON retire that connection and reject pending calls; reconnection does not replay failed work. Frame maximum is 2,097,152 bytes; newline counts for line frames, four-byte prefix is separate for length frames. Do not copy stale client code or claim remote middleware skipping/context injection is supported.

Docs parity means no badges, ignored legacy isPublic/IsPublic, schema/header descriptions and private configured-option values excluded. Node global docs env names differ from Go DOCS_ENABLED/DOCS_PATH. Auth remains application middleware in both; Go middleware schemas do not introduce runtime validation.

docs.title: Edit and run an application
docs.text:
example is the reference app. After building the core, run pnpm --dir example dev. Its functions/middlewares import workspace packages. A real generated project instead installs the public SDK. To evaluate local SDK changes in that project, pack the local SDK and select it explicitly in a disposable manifest; do not commit that override or claim it was a registry-only install.

Read the generated tests and auth customization before deploying anything. Avoid changing the example's routes incidentally while fixing core behavior.

docs.title: Documentation workflow
docs.text:
python3 -m venv /tmp/crpc-docs-venv
/tmp/crpc-docs-venv/bin/python -m pip install mkdocs-material

Root community policies are included by PyMdown snippets, so run MkDocs from the repository root.

For a targeted fix, choose a test first, then follow the source map. Report unavailable runtimes/platform checks explicitly. Keep generated dist, uploads, node_modules and local agent edits out of the PR. The sibling Go setup is independent: Go development.

docs.title: Functions and contracts
docs.text:
A namespace maps to directories below functionsDir. Each function exports contracts, optional middleware attachments and a named or default run handler. Use the generator to create the current layout; imports below use emitted .js paths so the examples also compile under NodeNext.

import { Type, type Static } from '@sinclair/typebox';
export const metadata = { description: 'Greet a named caller', tags: ['example'] };
export const contentType = 'application/json';
export const inputSchema = Type.Object({ name: Type.String({ minLength: 1 }) });
export const outputSchema = Type.Object({ greeting: Type.String() });
export type Input = Static<typeof inputSchema>;
export type Output = Static<typeof outputSchema>;

import type { MiddlewareContext } from '@cellsweb/rpc-core';
import type { Input, Output } from './constants.js';
export async function run(input: Input, _context: MiddlewareContext): Promise<Output> {
  return { greeting: `Hello, ${input.name}!` };
}

import { defineMiddlewares } from '@cellsweb/rpc-core';
export const middlewares = defineMiddlewares([{ name: 'auth', options: { role: 'reader' } }]);

The last block belongs to a protected function; the basic hello handler can run without it. The attachment refers to an application middleware module. It executes before input validation and the handler; output validation still runs before success. The framework exports MiddlewareContext, not a Context type. Request identity must be populated by verified middleware, not trusted from remote request data.

metadata may describe the function, tags and deprecation. The optional legacy FunctionMetadata.isPublic remains deprecated and ignored. It controls no docs visibility, authentication, registration or execution. New modules omit it.

HTTP data preserves object/array/scalar/null shape. Omitted data defaults to an empty object; a nullable string union therefore rejects omission but accepts explicit null. Schemas define which shapes a handler accepts.

docs.title: Released versions and prerequisites
docs.text: Release versions: @cellsweb/rpc-core@1.0.35, @cellsweb/rpc-client@1.0.26, create-cellsweb-rpc-api@1.0.31. Node 24 LTS is primary; the declared floor is Node 24.0.0. Bun 1.3.11 is tested separately for Bun/Elysia execution.

docs.title: Scaffold a project
docs.text:
npm create cellsweb-rpc-api@latest my-api -- --framework=node --yes
cd my-api
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run dev

For an exact initializer version use npx create-cellsweb-rpc-api@1.0.31 my-api --framework=node --yes. Choose bun|elysia|express|fastify|hono|node|ultimate-express as framework. For automation add --skip-install, then install the generated manifest yourself. Generated applications require core^1.0.34, resolved from public npm; no local SDK tarball or checkout is necessary. For Bun, use the selected Bun template and run its CLI under Bun when native Bun execution is wanted.

For an existing application, install only the package needed:

npm install @cellsweb/rpc-core@1.0.35
# In a client project:
npm install @cellsweb/rpc-client@1.0.26

The scaffold contains src/server.ts, src/env.ts, src/functions, src/middlewares, utilities, schemas and sample tests. Replace the sample authentication logic with your application's credential verification before relying on it.

curl http://localhost:4000/rpc -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"namespace":"public","functionName":"hello","data":{"name":"Alice"}}'

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The generated src/env.ts loads .env through dotenv; exported process values win. It parses numeric settings and booleans before passing them to CoreRPC. The default host/port are 0.0.0.0:4000. API_PORT, API_HOST, body/file limits, upload settings and telemetry are documented in the generated env module.

Generated docs are enabled outside production. In production they require parsed API_DOCS_ENABLED=true (trimmed/case-insensitive true/false/1/0; invalid falls back to false). Outside production the template deliberately keeps docs enabled even if this env flag is false; set application docs:false to disable them.

Direct new CoreRPC(...) reads process env, not dotenv. Explicit docs, docsEndpoint, rpcEndpoint, host/port options win. Raw-core production docs require exact string API_DOCS_ENABLED=true; outside production default is true. API_RPC_ENDPOINT, API_DOCS_ENDPOINT, API_HEALTH_ENDPOINT provide defaults. See global docs controls for disabled routes and privacy.

Build for deployment with npm run build, then npm start. The CLI start command sets NODE_ENV=production. Review docs exposure explicitly. All registered functions execute under the same middleware regardless of deprecated isPublic.

docs.title: Interactive documentation
docs.text: The documentation index lists every registered function and middleware. Function pages show input/output contracts, descriptions, tags, deprecation status and the attached middleware pipeline. Middleware cards and detail pages show option and header names, types, descriptions, nested fields and required/optional status. Required headers appear in function header tables and cURL placeholders for both JSON and multipart calls. Optional headers remain documented without becoming mandatory in the examples. Middleware links respect a custom docs endpoint.

docs.title: Global configuration
docs.text:
Use new CoreRPC({ docs: false }) to disable documentation, or configure docsEndpoint to change its path (default /docs). Explicit application options take precedence over environment values. Direct CoreRPC construction enables docs outside production; in production it requires API_DOCS_ENABLED to equal the string true. API_DOCS_ENDPOINT supplies the default docs path.

CLI-generated servers use their existing typed environment module and production guard. That module parses supported boolean strings before passing an explicit docs option. Disabling documentation blocks index, function and middleware pages; it does not unregister functions or change RPC execution.

The generated boolean parser accepts trimmed, case-insensitive true/false/1/0; invalid values fall back to false. Outside production the template keeps docs enabled even for an env false value; an explicit application docs:false disables them everywhere. Dotenv does not overwrite process exports. Raw CoreRPC does not load dotenv or use that parser. Go generated servers instead use exported DOCS_ENABLED/DOCS_PATH, reject invalid nonblank booleans and do not load .env.

Index, function and middleware detail pages share the global switch. With docs disabled, related docs/metadata/schema paths do not expose documentation. Query parameters and custom docs endpoints work in native and Fetch handlers. Unknown docs paths retain the existing Node index fallback; Go retains404.

docs.title: Public schema metadata and private configuration
docs.text:
The UI documents schemas, never per-function middleware option values. It does not read or serialize those configured values, even when a middleware has no schema. Middleware schema defaults, examples, constants, enum values and private extensions are omitted from the public projection, including nested schemas. Types, descriptions, required fields and structural constraints remain visible. Function input/output contracts retain their existing rendering.

Keep secrets out of names, descriptions and other public schema metadata. The renderer cannot classify secrets deliberately written into public prose or constraints. Metadata rendering does not mutate schemas, apply defaults, execute middleware or introduce validation. Existing execution-time behavior is unchanged.

docs.title: Deprecated metadata compatibility
docs.text:
FunctionMetadata.isPublic?: boolean is retained for existing typed user code. It is deprecated and ignored: it has no documentation visibility, authentication or authorization meaning. Omitted, true and false values have the same framework behavior. PUBLIC/PRIVATE badges have been removed; new generators and examples omit this field. No replacement visibility flag exists. The property may be removed in a future major release.

Go follows the same documentation policy. Its existing rpc.FunctionMetadata.IsPublic bool remains zero-value compatible; middleware documentation uses rpc.MiddlewareMetadata and native schema.SchemaRule values.

docs.title: Middleware and authentication
docs.text:
Middleware receives ({headers, options, function}, context) and returns the context for the next stage. Use the registered middleware name to namespace application state. Credential/session verification and authorization are the application's responsibility; the framework does not supply a JWT provider.

import { Type } from '@sinclair/typebox';
export const metadata = { description: 'Verify a bearer session and required role' };
export const optionsSchema = Type.Object({ role: Type.Optional(Type.String()) });
export const headersSchema = Type.Object({ authorization: Type.Optional(Type.String()) });

import { AppError, ErrorCode, type MiddlewareFn } from '@cellsweb/rpc-core';
type Session = { userId: string; role: string };
// Application integration point. This example denies until you implement it.
async function verifySession(_token: string): Promise<Session | null> { return null; }
export const run: MiddlewareFn<{ role?: string }, { auth: Session }> = async (
  { headers, options }, context,
) => {
  const raw = headers.authorization;
  if (typeof raw !== 'string' || !raw.startsWith('Bearer '))
    throw new AppError(ErrorCode.UNAUTHORIZED, 'Bearer credentials required');
  const session = await verifySession(raw.slice(7));
  if (!session) throw new AppError(ErrorCode.UNAUTHORIZED, 'Invalid credentials');
  if (options.role && session.role !== options.role)
    throw new AppError(ErrorCode.FORBIDDEN, 'Insufficient role');
  return { ...context, auth: session };
};

Attach middleware with defineMiddlewares in a function's middlewares.ts. The Node pipeline validates its declared options/headers, then invokes it in attachment order. Missing configured middleware fails closed. Header schemas are contracts; mark authorization optional when the middleware should issue its own unauthorized response rather than a header-schema validation error.

HTTP/IPC callers forward credentials in headers. There is no supported remote skipMiddlewares or trusted context injection option. A browser/SSR session object sent as JSON remains untrusted application data. Local test context helpers are not a remote authentication interface.

Go uses the same auth responsibilities but native schema.SchemaRule metadata; Go middleware option/header schemas document contracts without adding automatic runtime validation. Go middleware must validate what it needs explicitly.

Docs show schemas, descriptions and required headers, never configured option values/defaults. Keep secrets out of public descriptions. Deprecated isPublic has no authorization meaning and is ignored.

docs.title: Release and migration
docs.text:
Documentation patch versions: core 1.0.35, client 1.0.26 and scaffolder 1.0.31. Runtime implementations, public APIs and dependencies are unchanged from core1.0.34/client1.0.25/scaffolder1.0.30. Install the documentation patches from public npm; no local tarball substitution is needed. These supersede core 1.0.33/client 1.0.23/scaffolder 1.0.29 for this hardening release. Preserve the following migration notes when upgrading an existing application.

Node 24 LTS is primary, with declared/tested floor 24.0.0. Bun 1.3.11 is tested independently. The engine policy is explicit; no shim or older-runtime guarantee was added. Review package-manager engine-strict behavior when upgrading tooling.

Unions now enforce their declared branches, including nullable primitives and file constraints. Invalid values return validation_error; explicitly declare intended inputs instead of relying on the previous wildcard. Omitted HTTP data remains {}, explicit null remains null subject to the input schema.

Remove deprecated isPublic from new metadata; existing optional fields remain ignored. All registered functions may appear in globally enabled docs. There are no PUBLIC/PRIVATE badges or replacement visibility flags. Authentication and authorization remain middleware responsibilities; do not use caller context or middleware-skip examples. Forward credentials in headers.

Review generated server changes manually if you customized adapters. All seven templates preserve JSON, multipart routing consistency, bounds and cleanup; production docs require explicit enablement. Direct raw-core and generated env parsing differ as documented in configuration.

Go v1.0.2 adds bounded stdio framing. Install its versioned CLI to generate an SDK v1.0.2 dependency. A source/VCS-built Go CLI still selects the older v1.0.0 fallback; use an explicit workspace only when intentionally testing a local SDK checkout. IPC connection failures reject pending calls without automatic replay; Unix framing remains 2 MiB with documented delimiter rules.

docs.title: Schemas
docs.text:
Node uses TypeBox for runtime contracts. Input is checked before the handler and output before success. Unions accept only declared branches; nullable is different from optional.

import { Type, type Static } from '@sinclair/typebox';
import { File, Files, FormBool, FormNum, type UploadedFile } from '@cellsweb/rpc-core';

export const nullableText = Type.Union([Type.String(), Type.Null()]);
export const record = Type.Object({ note: Type.Optional(nullableText) });

export const upload = Type.Object({
  avatar: File({ mimeTypes: ['image/png'], maxSizeBytes: 5 * 1024 * 1024 }),
  attachments: Type.Optional(Files({ maxCount: 3, maxSizeBytes: 1024 * 1024 })),
  age: FormNum({ minimum: 18 }),
  accepted: FormBool(),
});

export type UploadInput = Static<typeof upload>;

export async function handleUpload(input: UploadInput) {
  const avatar: UploadedFile = input.avatar;
  const age: number = input.age;             // primitive number
  const accepted: boolean = input.accepted; // primitive boolean
  return { filename: avatar.filename, age, accepted };
}

An omitted object property may be optional. Explicit null must have a null branch when its contract requires one. Omitted HTTP data defaults to {}; it is not automatically converted to null. Nested ordinary JSON arrays/objects are valid.

File() and Files() check physical UploadedFile instances plus configured size/MIME/count rules. File unions retain non-file branches and reject unrelated values; file defaults/transforms do not remove these checks. TypeBox JSON Schema metadata alone is not content sanitization. Declared/detected MIME is heuristic.

docs.title: Multipart Form Helpers: FormNum and FormBool
docs.text:
In multipart form uploads (multipart/form-data / browser FormData), RFC 7578 transmits every non-file form field as a textual string. Standard TypeBox schemas like Type.Number() and Type.Boolean() strictly reject string values during schema validation.

FormNum() and FormBool() bridge this gap by providing TypeBox transforms designed for multipart intake: - They accept string representations from multipart form fields and decode them into JavaScript primitive types (number and boolean) before passing the sanitized data object to the application handler. - They also accept native JSON numbers and booleans directly when invoked via standard JSON requests. - Ordinary JSON schemas do not acquire blanket transport coercion; FormNum() and FormBool() are explicit opt-in helpers.

docs.title: Accepted Values and Handler Types
docs.text:
Helper Accepted FormData Strings Handler-Received Type Example Valid Inputs Example Invalid Inputs FormNum(options?) Numeric strings matching /^-?\d+(\.\d+)?$/ number "42", "-7", "3.14", 0 "abc", "", "42px" FormBool(options?) Exact "true" or "false" strings boolean "true", "false", true, false "invalid", "1", "0", "yes"

FormNum() supports standard TypeBox numeric constraints: minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, and multipleOf.

docs.title: Validation Errors and Error Envelope
docs.text:
When input fails validation (such as non-numeric text for FormNum(), a value below minimum, or an invalid boolean string), the server rejects the request before the handler executes. Under the framework's uniform architecture, handled application errors return HTTP 200 OK by default with an RPC error envelope:

{
  "status": "error",
  "code": "validation_error",
  "message": "Validation failed",
  "details": [
    {
      "path": "/age",
      "message": "Expected number >= 18, got 16"
    }
  ]
}

Handled validation errors preserve the uniform HTTP 200 default contract rather than throwing unhandled transport errors. Applications requiring conventional HTTP error statuses can optionally configure useHttpStatusCodes: true on CoreRPC.

docs.title: General Guidelines
docs.text:
File transport supports top-level fields and direct file arrays only; nested files inside objects remain unsupported.

Use TypeBox's normal constraints/defaults for other types. Register any custom formats your application uses; an arbitrary format name is not a built-in email verifier. Unknown/extra properties follow the actual schema and may differ from Go's native strict-object rules. Do not claim every TypeBox keyword is a native Go schema feature. Avoid large-integer precision assumptions across JavaScript.

docs.title: Report privately
docs.text:
Please report suspected vulnerabilities through GitHub private vulnerability reporting when the repository's Security tab offers Report a vulnerability. Availability is a repository setting; opening a public issue is not a fallback for sensitive reports.

If the private form is unavailable, use info@cellsweb.com or the official contact page to request a private reporting channel. Send only a brief nonsensitive request until a suitable channel is confirmed. Do not post exploit details in public issues, discussions, pull requests, logs or chat transcripts.

docs.title: What to include in a private report
docs.text:
• Affected repository, package/module version, runtime and operating system.
  • A minimal reproducible example, prerequisites and expected/actual behavior.
  • Security impact and the trust boundary crossed; identify HTTP, multipart, in-memory or IPC paths and whether authentication is required.
  • Relevant sanitized requests/responses and the earliest known affected version. Use dummy credentials and files, not customer data, keys or production secrets.

Allow maintainers to reproduce and coordinate a fix before public disclosure. Discuss disclosure timing privately; this policy does not promise an invented acknowledgment deadline or backport schedule. Maintainers will determine affected versions and release guidance during triage.

docs.title: Release context and responsibilities
docs.text:
The release-line installation guides and changelogs identify package/module versions. Include your exact installed versions when reporting, including older versions if relevant. There is no published long-term-support matrix here.

Application middleware owns credential verification and authorization. Generated auth modules are customization examples. Deprecated isPublic/IsPublic metadata is ignored, and docs availability is globally configured. These facts do not exclude genuine framework bypasses, data exposure or resource-exhaustion reports.

For ordinary nonsensitive bugs use the bug template. Conduct concerns follow the Code of Conduct.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
createTestCaller exercises the in-memory pipeline, not an HTTP listener. call unwraps data/throws AppError; callRaw returns the application envelope. Neither skips authentication or schema validation. Supply test credentials in headers and an application verifier fixture that recognizes them.

import { CoreRPC, createTestCaller } from '@cellsweb/rpc-core';
export async function testHello() {
  const app = new CoreRPC({ functionsDir: './dist/functions', middlewaresDir: './dist/middlewares', docs: false });
  const caller = createTestCaller(app, { headers: { authorization: 'Bearer test-credential' } });
  const result = await caller.callRaw('public.hello', { name: 'Test' });
  await app.close();
  return result;
}

There is no app.init() method; getRegistry/createHandler/fetch/execute load the registry as needed. Local context overrides are controlled test facilities, not a transport interface or an authorization bypass.

Source validation: pnpm build, pnpm typecheck, pnpm test. Generated projects use npm run typecheck, npm run build, npm test. Live HTTP tests are also needed for socket draining, multipart disconnect/cleanup, headers and adapter intake; an in-memory test cannot establish transport behavior.

crpc test:audit invokes Vitest with verbose/JSON reporters and writes audit-reports/security-audit.json. It does not discover every function's auth policy, create an HTML security certificate, or independently certify security.

docs.title: Multipart uploads
docs.text:
The client converts top-level File/Blob values or React Native {uri,name,type} assets, and direct file arrays, into multipart when multipart:true is selected. Nested file-in-object inputs are rejected; they are not silently serialized.

import { createRpcClient } from '@cellsweb/rpc-client';
const rpc = createRpcClient({ baseUrl: 'http://localhost:4000/rpc' });
export async function uploadAvatar(avatar: File) {
  return rpc.request({ namespace: 'user', functionName: 'uploadAvatar',
    multipart: true, data: { avatar } });
}

import { Type, type Static } from '@sinclair/typebox';
import { File } from '@cellsweb/rpc-core';
export const contentType = 'multipart/form-data';
export const inputSchema = Type.Object({ avatar: File({ maxSizeBytes: 5 * 1024 * 1024 }) });
export const outputSchema = Type.Object({ filename: Type.String(), bytes: Type.Number() });
export type Input = Static<typeof inputSchema>;

import type { Input } from './constants.js';
export async function run(input: Input) {
  return { filename: input.avatar.filename, bytes: input.avatar.byteLength };
}

Node UploadedFile has path, filename, mimeType, declaredMimeType, detectedMimeType, byteLength, createReadStream(), toBuffer() and toBlob(). It does not expose filepath, mimetype or size. Use the generated storage helper or application-owned unique destinations for persistence. Do not use a raw client filename as a trusted destination. Complete persistence during the handler; framework-owned temporary files are cleaned when processing finishes.

When submitting non-file form fields alongside file uploads (such as ages, flags, or counts), use FormNum() and FormBool() in inputSchema so textual multipart field values are decoded into primitive numbers and booleans; see Schemas.

Both routing headers (X-CRPC-Namespace/X-CRPC-Function) or neither are allowed. When present they must agree with redundant body routing fields. Headerless routing remains supported; put routing text fields before files. Authentication preflight must not create application-owned temporary files for denied requests.

Native Node/Express/Fastify/Ultimate Express use stream intake with Busboy. Fetch formData in Bun/Hono/Elysia may buffer at runtime. Go fasthttp buffers transport intake before application multipart processing. Per-request limits and cleanup are not an aggregate-memory or zero-buffering guarantee.

docs.title: Worker execution
docs.text:
Functions can export worker = true to opt into the existing worker path. Keep handlers transport-neutral and use serializable inputs/results. A worker is not an authorization bypass: middleware and input/output checks still apply.

export const worker = true;
export async function run(input: { values: number[] }) {
  return { total: input.values.reduce((sum, value) => sum + value, 0) };
}

Define schemas alongside the handler and build source for the selected runtime. Do not send live HTTP objects, database connections or temporary upload handles through a worker boundary. Configure application-owned resources explicitly. Worker scheduling does not promise parallel speedup for every workload or replace upload/body bounds. Test worker functions on the deployment runtime; generated HTTP adapter smoke tests are not a benchmark or every-worker-feature matrix.

docs.title: Node architecture and source map
docs.text: Start here when implementing a change. Read shared contracts, then trace one request. Public usage stays in the user guides; these pages describe actual released internals, not a proposed refactor.

docs.title: Design and package ownership
docs.text:
Functions have a route key, schema contracts and a transport-neutral handler. Middleware enriches trusted context. Parsers adapt transport input; the pipeline owns validation/dispatch; wrappers own response serialization and file cleanup. Node and Go intentionally use different native implementations.
